title: Whats Taking You So Long to Decide
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article defends leaders' apparent slowness to decide as a rational response to volatile conditions rather than avoidance or weakness. It argues team members prize decisiveness because clarity makes execution easier, but leaders apply a different calculus, knowing that committing to a decision forecloses other options in an environment that keeps shifting. The piece frames the resulting tension between urgency and optionality as productive: team members' impatience pushes leaders to act before problems worsen, while leaders' instinct to preserve options guards against premature commitments that fail as conditions change. It concludes that this dynamic, while a source of frustration on both sides, ultimately produces better decisions than either urgency or caution alone.
points: Team members equate decisiveness with good leadership, but leaders often deliberately preserve optionality in fast-changing environments.
Once a leader commits to a decision, other options effectively disappear - which is why leaders resist deciding prematurely.
The tension between team members' desire for clarity and leaders' desire for optionality is productive when balanced well.
Team members' impatience serves a purpose: it pressures leaders to act before problems compound or opportunities vanish.
Waiting for the last responsible moment to decide allows leaders to account for a decision's full implications and unintended consequences.
quotes: If it were up to any given team member, leaders would just decide and move forward.
To those waiting for a decision, it appears that leaders often do everything in their power not to make one.
When a leader commits to a decision, all the other options disappear.
Good decision-makers don’t commit to a path until they have to. That’s what good leaders believe.
Quality decisions benefit from both urgency and optionality.
Leaders who remain steadfast in their commitment to keep their options open usually make better decisions.
Yet another reason why leadership is both thankless and hard.
